Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Slaty gnateater (Conopophaga ardesiaca) were obtained through respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 70.91 milliliters per hour [JOi = 70.91 milliliters per hour], a value that aligns reasonably well with predictions for a suboscine passerine of this body size. This metabolic rate likely reflects the energetic demands of a sedentary, insectivorous foraging strategy typical of understory-dwelling members of the Conopophagidae family. The measurement was taken from post-absorptive, inactive individuals during their natural rest phase to ensure basal conditions were met. Several individuals were measured repeatedly across multiple days, and the highest recorded value was selected to represent the species' peak metabolic capacity under thermoneutral conditions. These data contribute to a growing comparative dataset on the metabolic physiology of Neotropical forest birds, which remain underrepresented in the literature.

The initial wet body mass at hatching, based on data from the closely related Conopophaga peruviana, is estimated at 2.7 grams [Ww0 = 2.7 grams]. Newly hatched nestlings are altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning, emerging from eggs that weigh a fraction of this neonatal mass. Females ultimately reach a considerably larger size, with the maximum adult wet weight recorded at 26.3 grams [Wwi = 26.3 grams], more than nine times the hatchling mass. This substantial growth trajectory is typical of forest-dwelling passerines and requires a steady supply of arthropod prey delivered by both parents during the nestling period. The pronounced difference between initial and adult mass underscores the rapid somatic development that occurs during the early weeks of life, a phase critical for achieving the body condition necessary for successful fledging. Such growth parameters are essential for constructing accurate life-history profiles for this relatively poorly known species.

Eggs incubated at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] require a mean incubation period of 13.5 days [ab = 13.5 days] before hatching. This duration, which falls within the typical range for small-bodied passerines, reflects the thermal conditions under which embryonic development proceeds. Under the warmer thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which corresponds to the species' active metabolic temperature, the developmental timeline becomes more compressed. After hatching, the nestling period culminates in fledging, which occurs at 14.5 days since birth [tx = 14.5 days since birth] when maintained at 40.2 °C at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief nestling phase is characteristic of species that face high nest predation risk in dense understory habitats. The synchrony of hatching and the rapid feather development observed in this species suggest strong selective pressure for early departure from the nest, even at the cost of incomplete flight proficiency.

Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is achieved at 43.5 days since birth [tp = 43.5 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This age at sexual maturity is quite early for a Neotropical passerine of this size, suggesting that individuals may begin breeding in the same season they hatched if environmental conditions are favorable. Females produce approximately 3.9 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3.9 eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size that may be linked to the energetic constraints of provisioning a single nestling in a competitive understory environment. The annual reproductive rhythm yields approximately 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches each year], a frequency that allows for multiple breeding attempts should earlier nests fail. This combination of early maturation and iterative nesting represents a bet-hedging strategy common among tropical forest birds facing unpredictable predation regimes and fluctuating food availability throughout the year.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under field conditions is 6 years [am = 6 years] when measured at the species' active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that of other small-bodied suboscines from stable tropical environments. First reproduction typically occurs at 1.1 years since birth [tR = 1.1 years since birth] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], indicating that some individuals defer breeding until their second year, possibly due to constraints related to territory establishment or mate acquisition. The delay between reaching puberty at approximately 43.5 days and first breeding at over a year suggests a prolonged period of social and physiological preparation. Across its range, the Slaty gnateater maintains a conservative life-history strategy characterized by low annual fecundity and relatively high adult survival. Such demographic parameters are consistent with a population that is sensitive to habitat disturbance and slow to recover from environmental perturbations.
